title: Current assessment of all 59 Solomon and Freeman baseline propositions
status: First complete assessment for author review; not finished-book approval
coverage: Consolidates all seven substantive chapters and their stable case dossiers. Each dossier controls its event cutoff and reading scope; the assessment date does not imply complete 2026 coverage.

status_definitions.retain within tested scope: The specified component is directly supported within the examined episodes. This does not retain every causal, comparative or cultural element of the full baseline proposition.
status_definitions.revise or narrow: The proposition requires an explicit restriction or reformulation for this corpus. A scope correction is not necessarily evidence of temporal change.
status_definitions.correct baseline: A proposition-level baseline statement is factually wrong on the acquired evidence. No entire behavioral proposition receives this status here; separate factual corrections are linked below.
status_definitions.unresolved: Relevant observations or candidate mechanisms exist, but the available evidence does not decide a consequential part of the proposition.
status_definitions.untested: The acquired corpus contains no adequate case-level test of the specified mechanism. Absence of a test is not evidence against it.

interpretation_rules: The baseline claim and its original extraction fields are preserved verbatim. They are the research inventory’s paraphrases, not presented as verbatim sentences from the book; short direct quotations are identified separately.

Original baseline caveats may describe access at the time of extraction. Current evidence entries and linked dossiers control later acquisitions; preserving the original record does not erase those subsequent reads.
A verdict applies to the tested component. The complete proposition remains visible so that retaining a practice does not silently retain an unproved mechanism or general effect.

Supporting evidence can establish only a component or supply an attributed hypothesis. Contrary or limiting evidence can be a failed expectation, competing mechanism, counterpart practice or a limit of access; it is not automatically a falsification.

Source IDs within one entry are not independent votes. Reprinted official texts, related editions, shared interview chains and cases reused across propositions are not counted as independent corroboration.

Contemporary accepted instruments establish terms more directly than private motive. Readouts establish positions and reported encounters; retrospective participant and scholarly accounts retain their documented source-chain limits.
Formal acceptance, legal obligation, implementation, and later disputes are distinct observations. The full S-P25 asymmetry is not inferred from continuation alone.

No matched representative sample supports national uniqueness, general frequency, comparative predictor reliability or a clean historical effect. A new instrument type is not itself proof of a changed national preference.
This is a consolidation of registered source reading, not a fresh full reading of every referenced source or an acquisition of underlying private records.

An original qualification is not a new behavioral revision. Failure to establish a frequency, comparative ranking or causal mechanism receives an unresolved verdict; caution in practical use is stated separately from empirical falsification.

factual_corrections.scope: Treaty identification, normalization date and Geng Biao’s office are corrected separately. These errors do not by themselves refute the associated behavioral mechanisms; zero whole-proposition correct-baseline verdicts must not be read as zero factual errors.

baseline.author: Solomon
baseline.claim: Chinese negotiating style varies with the political purpose of the relationship: officials can use markedly different approaches in confrontation and in constructing cooperation.
baseline.evidence_type: Cross-period comparison of American memoirs, interviews, and the official negotiating record; explicit scope qualification
baseline.evidence_details: Contrasts the 1950s–1960s experience described by Young, Joy, Dean, Johnson, and Beam with the normalization experience, sometimes involving the same Chinese officials. At p24 n7 Solomon leaves applicability to a future confrontation unanswered.
baseline.test: Compare the same officials and comparable issues across cooperative and confrontational periods; determine whether changes follow strategic purpose, personnel, or institutions. A stable approach independent of relationship purpose would weaken the proposition.
baseline.caveat: The principal study covers a selected setting in which Beijing wanted a positive U.S. relationship. Different behavior after 2018 need not mean the original findings were wrong within that scope. The cited underlying records have not been independently acquired in this workstream.

baseline_scope.author_period_and_domain: Principal empirical period 1967–1984, principally American–Chinese high political negotiation while Beijing sought a constructive relationship; application to future confrontation was explicitly left open. The claim-specific qualification below also applies.
baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: The principal study covers a selected setting in which Beijing wanted a positive U.S. relationship. Different behavior after 2018 need not mean the original findings were wrong within that scope. The cited underlying records have not been independently acquired in this workstream.

assessments.tested_component: Whether differences in negotiating conduct follow the political purpose of the relationship, rather than the issue, channel, personnel or institution.

supporting_evidence.observation: Diplomatic contact reopened while defense access remained unavailable; later specified cooperation coexisted with political disagreement.
supporting_evidence.limit: This establishes channel-specific variation, not a matched comparison isolating relationship purpose.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: Close political relations did not settle successive gas projects.
contrary_or_limiting_evidence.limit: Relationship purpose does not determine individual commercial terms.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: Keep Solomon’s original restriction to a constructive relationship as a boundary on interpretation. The later cases show variation but do not identify political purpose as its cause; the central comparative claim remains unresolved. Confrontation is not automatic refutation of the cooperation-era baseline.

baseline.author: Solomon
baseline.claim: Chinese domestic social and political traditions help produce a persistent preference for managing negotiation through personal relationships and reciprocal obligations.
baseline.evidence_type: Cultural-historical causal interpretation supported by participant accounts and secondary social-science literature
baseline.evidence_details: Links contemporary relationship cultivation to guanxi and earlier diplomatic practices, while also identifying Western and Soviet influences and continued adaptation.
baseline.test: Compare Chinese institutions, generations, counterpart countries, and private versus state negotiations; test whether relationship dependence persists after controlling for information scarcity, weak formal enforcement, access to authority, and bargaining power.
baseline.caveat: Observed use of relationships does not identify culture as its cause. The study assumed distinctive style would be legible to foreign observers; unfamiliarity and observer expectations can influence that assessment.

assessments.tested_component: Persistence of relationship cultivation; cultural origin separated from its observable use.

supporting_evidence.observation: Xi and Wang publicly honored Kissinger and sought a constructive contribution.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: No U.S. mission mandate was acknowledged; consultation existed without a specified policy effect.
contrary_or_limiting_evidence.limit: Neither record identifies cultural causation.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: Need comparative decisions linking reciprocal obligations to changed conduct, controlling for policy affinity, reputation, information and access. Persistence is not a test of its cultural explanation.

baseline.author: Solomon
baseline.claim: Chinese negotiators resist terms or public presentations that depict China as dependent, even when material conditions create a need for foreign cooperation.
baseline.evidence_type: Named memcons and drafting episodes combined with a status/dependence interpretation
baseline.evidence_details: Zhou–Kissinger, July 9–11, 1971, on reciprocity and the visit announcement; the liaison-office discussion; Kissinger–Huang Hua, September 19, 1972, and Solomon–Ji Chaozhu, October 25, 1974, on grain; Deng–Kissinger, October 20, 1975, and Mao–Kissinger, October 21, 1975, on strategic need.
baseline.test: Track concrete wording disputes, who sought meetings, private admissions of need, and resulting concessions. Compare episodes where Beijing accepted publicly asymmetric dependence with those where it paid a cost to avoid it.
baseline.caveat: The chapter itself records acknowledgment of mutual need and prior acceptance of a subordinate Soviet relationship. National humiliation and imperial status are proposed explanations, not directly observed motives in every episode.

baseline.author: Solomon
baseline.claim: Chinese officials exploit existing political or bureaucratic rivalries by favoring counterparts whose preferences better match Chinese objectives and making others fear a loss of influence.
baseline.evidence_type: Comparative episode interpretation and practical recommendation
baseline.evidence_details: Vance/Brzezinski, Kissinger/Schlesinger, and Haig/Allen comparisons. Solomon explicitly says Beijing did not create the rivalries in these examples.
baseline.test: Reconstruct the rivals' policy preferences before cultivation, differential Chinese access or messages, and any subsequent change in internal authority or instructions; test cases where a coordinated government neutralized the maneuver.
baseline.caveat: Selecting a receptive channel is not the same as changing a government's preferences. American rivalries are part of the explanation and cannot be coded solely as Chinese tactical success.

baseline.author: Solomon
baseline.claim: Uncertainty over meetings with senior Chinese leaders can be used to induce foreign counterparts to clarify intentions or accommodate Chinese conditions.
baseline.evidence_type: Named memcon, observed scheduling, and explicitly speculative attribution
baseline.evidence_details: Zhou–Kissinger, July 9, 1971, on conditions surrounding a Nixon–Mao meeting; unexpected timing of Nixon's and Ford's Mao meetings; the canceled second Nixon–Mao meeting.
baseline.test: Compare scheduling records, medical constraints, instructions, and draft meeting conditions with concessions made before access was granted; establish intentional linkage rather than mere timing correlation.
baseline.caveat: Solomon expressly speculates that the second Nixon meeting was canceled over Taiwan; illness was the Chinese explanation. That case cannot be counted as proven tactical manipulation.

baseline.author: Solomon
baseline.claim: In high-level political negotiations, flexibility often requires senior authorization after the foreign position has been tested; senior intervention can release an apparent deadlock.
baseline.evidence_type: Negotiating-record synthesis and institutional causal interpretation
baseline.evidence_details: Zhou's consultation with Mao during early Kissinger exchanges; the chapter's general pattern of a senior figure intervening after subordinates display inflexibility.
baseline.test: Locate draft instructions and approval sequences; determine whether concessions preceded or followed leadership decisions, whether delegates already possessed authority, and whether a deadlock was staged or reflected genuine disagreement.
baseline.caveat: A leader's visible intervention does not prove that lack of prior authorization caused delay. Issue stakes, tactical theater, and substantive incompatibility remain alternatives.

baseline.author: Solomon
baseline.claim: Chinese political negotiators tend to prefer broad understandings and principles to exhaustive legal detail, but can set principles aside or rationalize concrete compromise when agreement serves their interests.
baseline.evidence_type: Interview and negotiating-record synthesis, with explicit exceptions
baseline.evidence_details: Summary discussion of principles at p5; comparison of public political understandings with American legal/technical preferences at p170; claims/assets example at p173.
baseline.test: Track the specificity and legal form each side requests, revisions to principles, and actual constraints principles impose on concessions. Compare issue types, delegates, and legal institutions rather than coding any general declaration as supporting evidence.
baseline.caveat: The study's high-political baseline is not a representative sample of commercial or technical negotiations. A principle that can always be overridden risks becoming an unfalsifiable explanation.

assessments.original_text_qualification: Freeman p. 183 presents the trust-building rationale as the Chinese view, then explicitly allows success in an appropriate context, failure and, continuing on p. 184, uncertain success. baseline.author: Freeman

baseline.author: Freeman

baseline.author: Freeman

baseline.claim: PRC officials try to channel important negotiations through sympathetic foreign decision makers with senior access, sometimes bypassing or separating less congenial officials and advisers.
baseline.evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; narrative reconstruction of personnel preferences; commercial anecdotes; author inference.
baseline.historical_anchor: Mao–Nixon, February 21, 1972; Chinese preference for Kissinger conveyed through intermediaries in early 1971; Vance–Huang Hua, September 28, 1977; subsequent Brzezinski channel.
baseline.test: Code requested participants, actual attendance, access to the top decision maker, channels excluded, and policy changes after rerouting. Distinguish routine protocol from unusual exclusion and test whether the preferred interlocutor actually grants more favorable terms.
baseline.caveat: Solomon acknowledges that governments generally prefer friendly counterparts. Presidential access, substantive anti-Soviet alignment, and decision authority are practical explanations alongside guanxi. Physical isolation examples are principally commercial and should not automatically be generalized to summit diplomacy.

baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: Solomon acknowledges that governments generally prefer friendly counterparts. Presidential access, substantive anti-Soviet alignment, and decision authority are practical explanations alongside guanxi. Physical isolation examples are principally commercial and should not automatically be generalized to summit diplomacy.

assessments.tested_component: Preferred interlocutors and senior access versus policy leverage through channel selection.

supporting_evidence.observation: Kissinger met senior Chinese leaders and a defense minister inaccessible through the sought official contact.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: His U.S. representation was explicitly denied; Xi had already met the serving secretary.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: Observed access is retained. Deliberate exclusion to influence internal U.S. competition and more favorable terms remain unestablished; do not turn retired advisory access into authority.

baseline.claim: Hosting negotiations and managing hospitality, protocol, timing, and uncertainty can give PRC officials influence over visitors' mood, fatigue, and perceived control.
baseline.evidence_type: Kissinger memoir passages; participant impressions; visit anecdotes; narrative comparison with older adversarial encounters.
baseline.historical_anchor: Kissinger's July and October 1971 visits; October 1975 communiqué discussions before Ford's visit; Nixon's staged Ming Tombs encounter and Ford's incorrectly selected university song.
baseline.test: Compare venues, control over schedules, delegation support, fatigue reports, and concessions. Seek documentation of intentional scheduling pressure. Test whether equivalent arrangements abroad or improved communications alter the pattern and whether repeated visitors become less susceptible.
baseline.caveat: The book gives practical reasons for Beijing venues, including communications and access to decision makers. It records gaffes and visitor suspicion. Kissinger expressly could not distinguish tactical delay from leadership review in July 1971; perceived manipulation is not proof of intent.

baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: The book gives practical reasons for Beijing venues, including communications and access to decision makers. It records gaffes and visitor suspicion. assessments.tested_component: Ceremonial setting and scheduling as causes of mood, fatigue or perceived control.

supporting_evidence.observation: The historical Diaoyutai setting was explicitly recognized by host and guest.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: Aircraft-return steps included material preparation and technical constraints.
contrary_or_limiting_evidence.limit: Time consumed cannot automatically be coded as deliberate exhaustion.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: Hospitality’s behavioral effects and intent are not reconstructed. Need contemporaneous visitor reactions connected to changed offers, and comparable venue/schedule controls.

baseline.claim: PRC negotiators seek advantageous agenda wording and sequencing, and may withhold discussion of other issues to press a priority demand or protect relationships with allies.
baseline.evidence_type: Memcon and intermediary-message excerpts; older negotiator memoirs; author reconstruction of agenda bargaining.
baseline.historical_anchor: Stoessel–Lei, January 20 and February 20, 1970; Kissinger–Hilaly messages, December 1970–May 1971; Zhou–Kissinger, July 9 and 11, 1971; unsuccessful pressure on Ford in 1975.
baseline.test: Record each side's initial agenda, changes, excluded topics, reasons given, and substantive outcome. Compare public and private agendas. Test whether topic linkage extracts concessions, stalls other cooperation, or protects an alliance without changing the counterpart's priority position.
baseline.caveat: The final normalization dialogue included the broader security issues Washington sought. Agenda pressure failed to secure normalization under Ford. The chapter also attributes agenda precision to narrow instructions and preparation requirements, not only deliberate manipulation.

baseline_scope.author_period_and_domain: Principal empirical period 1967–1984, principally American–Chinese high political negotiation while Beijing sought a constructive relationship; application to future confrontation was explicitly left open. The claim-specific qualification below also applies.
baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: The final normalization dialogue included the broader security issues Washington sought. Agenda pressure failed to secure normalization under Ford. The chapter also attributes agenda precision to narrow instructions and preparation requirements, not only deliberate manipulation.

assessments.tested_component: Observable agenda separation and conditional sequencing, without assuming successful coercion.

supporting_evidence.observation: Crew departure, a future meeting and aircraft arrangements were distinguished from responsibility and reconnaissance positions.
Access to particular contacts became a disputed object.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: Huawei was explicitly outside the partial trade agreement; agenda pressure did not absorb every issue into one bargain.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: The practice is documented; who proposed a sequence and whether withholding one topic caused a concession elsewhere often remain unknown. Universal uniqueness is untested.

baseline.claim: PRC political negotiators favor broad principles and flexible political documents, subsequently invoking those formulations to constrain the counterpart while retaining discretion over concrete arrangements.
baseline.evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; communiqué descriptions; Freeman's 1975 analysis cited by Solomon; author interpretation of agreement form.
baseline.historical_anchor: Deng–Bush, May 8, 1982; Huang Hua–Woodcock, July 7, 1978; Vance–Huang Hua, October 3, 1978; Shanghai and normalization communiqués; Zhao Ziyang's 1983 policy statement.
baseline.test: Compare opening principles with final provisions, document type, specificity, enforcement arrangements, and later assertions of obligation. Include technically detailed negotiations and formal treaties. Identify when principles are declined, reinterpreted, or set aside and whether compromise still occurs.
baseline.caveat: Solomon concedes agreements apparently inconsistent with early principles and American refusals to accept Chinese formulations. Relationship trust, uncertainty reduction, and tactical flexibility are competing explanations. A unilateral claim that a principle was violated is not proof of a mutually accepted obligation.

baseline_scope.author_period_and_domain: Principal empirical period 1967–1984, principally American–Chinese high political negotiation while Beijing sought a constructive relationship; application to future confrontation was explicitly left open. The claim-specific qualification below also applies.
baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: Solomon concedes agreements apparently inconsistent with early principles and American refusals to accept Chinese formulations. Relationship trust, uncertainty reduction, and tactical flexibility are competing explanations. A unilateral claim that a principle was violated is not proof of a mutually accepted obligation.

assessments.tested_component: The conjunction of preference for flexible political formulations, later invocation against the counterpart, and preservation of Chinese discretion.

supporting_evidence.observation: Public Chinese demands invoked principles and earlier assurances.
supporting_evidence.limit: This demonstrates framing and invocation, not shared acceptance of the asserted meaning or a change forced on the counterpart.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: A precise procedural agreement preserved avenues for continued legal dispute.
contrary_or_limiting_evidence.limit: A precise legal procedure can coexist with a preference for broad political understandings in other negotiations.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: Detailed review-process provisions existed before and within Phase One.
contrary_or_limiting_evidence.limit: Regulatory specificity does not independently test the claimed political preference or asymmetric use of accepted principles.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: The full preference-and-constraint mechanism remains unresolved. Principles are invoked, but public readouts do not establish a preferred alternative, original shared meaning, effective constraint or the alleged asymmetry in retained discretion. Recover linked drafts and responses; preserve the original political scope rather than treating it as a new correction.
assessments.original_text_qualification: Solomon p. 151 expressly discusses a preference in political agreements. His earlier discussion allows concrete compromise and refusal or violation of principles. The presence of legal or technical detail does not by itself narrow an unqualified universal claim, because that was not the original proposition.

baseline.claim: PRC negotiators often seek a comprehensive account of the counterpart's position before revealing their own, even when the host–guest justification changes with the venue.
baseline.evidence_type: Direct memcon excerpts; narrative descriptions of negotiating exchanges; explicit exception in footnote 21.
baseline.historical_anchor: Zhou–Kissinger, July 9, 1971; Huang Hua–Woodcock, July 5 and July 14, 1978; Geng–Brown, January 7, 1980; Kissinger–Qiao, October 8, 1976.
baseline.test: Code who presents the first substantive offer, who asks for further detail, whether presentation is reciprocal, and when Chinese instructions appear fixed. Compare informational advantage with the practical need to obtain a documented foreign position for superiors.
baseline.caveat: Footnote 21 says Chinese officials may present first when tasked with establishing a principle or limiting discussion. The behavior is an information-seeking convention, not sufficient evidence of a unique national characteristic or of concessions obtained.

baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: Footnote 21 says Chinese officials may present first when tasked with establishing a principle or limiting discussion. The behavior is an information-seeking convention, not sufficient evidence of a unique national characteristic or of concessions obtained.

assessments.tested_component: Obtaining the other side’s comprehensive opening position before disclosing China’s own, including host/guest rationales.
assessments.unresolved_remainder: No later paired transcript sample in this corpus tests speaking order and information gained. Final offers and leader readouts cannot substitute for the first-exchange sequence.

baseline.claim: PRC officials sometimes use underspecified formulations, analogies, indirect signals, or apparent misunderstanding to elicit a concrete response while limiting their own immediate commitment.
baseline.evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; memoir-based narrative; author interpretations of symbolism; one short subsection without a developed example.
baseline.historical_anchor: Stoessel–Lei Yang, February 20, 1970; Mao–Kissinger and Zhou–Kissinger, November 12–14, 1973; Zhou–Nixon, February 23, 1972; Ji Chaozhu–U.S. Embassy Officer, March 2, 1982.
baseline.test: Preserve literal Chinese and English wording before assigning a hidden meaning. Compare the counterpart's interpretation with later clarification, instructions, or offers. Test ambiguity against genuine uncertainty, translation problems, or limited authorization, and record unsuccessful or missed signals.
baseline.caveat: The chapter sometimes marks these meanings as conjectural. Its playing-dumb subsection lacks a dated illustrative case. Cultural explanations of indirection do not exclude ordinary exploratory bargaining, and both sides can overinterpret symbolism.

baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: The chapter sometimes marks these meanings as conjectural. Its playing-dumb subsection lacks a dated illustrative case. Cultural explanations of indirection do not exclude ordinary exploratory bargaining, and both sides can overinterpret symbolism.

assessments.tested_component: Intentional underspecification used to elicit a response while retaining discretion.

supporting_evidence.observation: Chinese public responses give limited detail on commercial gas arrangements.
supporting_evidence.limit: Sparse disclosure is only a candidate observation, not direct evidence of projective testing.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: The public account explicitly identifies no public office and names topics without operational details.
contrary_or_limiting_evidence.limit: Confidentiality, mandate limits and incomplete agreement explain omissions without a tactical probe.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: No dated probe–response–clarification chain establishes the proposed mechanism. Final-text precision neither verifies nor refutes indirect exploratory bargaining.

baseline.claim: Trusted intermediaries and lower-level or informal channels can convey sensitive positions, test ideas, and insulate senior leaders from direct confrontation.
baseline.evidence_type: Intermediary-message and memcon excerpts; official-channel descriptions; one explicitly personal recollection.
baseline.historical_anchor: Kissinger–Hilaly, December 9, 1970; Pakistan's role in the opening; Haig–Zhang Wenjin, September 22, 1981; Allen–Chai, October 2, 1981; Zhang–Hummel, December 4 and 22, 1981.
baseline.test: Map senders, carriers, audiences, authority, deniability, and subsequent incorporation into official positions. Compare intermediary selection with available alternatives. Test whether the channel reduces confrontation, communicates genuine flexibility, or simply duplicates the formal position.
baseline.caveat: Trust and guanxi coexist with secrecy, access, common interests, and availability. Footnote 36 explicitly compares informal exchanges with U.S.–Soviet practice. A reported private message does not establish authorized policy unless its provenance can be verified.

baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: Trust and guanxi coexist with secrecy, access, common interests, and availability. Footnote 36 explicitly compares informal exchanges with U.S.–Soviet practice. A reported private message does not establish authorized policy unless its provenance can be verified.

assessments.tested_component: Trusted-channel transmission and its effect, distinguished from access and ordinary consultation.

supporting_evidence.observation: Stern describes specialist trust and confidential preparation of bilateral climate announcements.
supporting_evidence.limit: One retrospective participant account.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: Public private-status denial, anticipated debrief and acknowledged advice provide no July message-to-instruction chain.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: Recover paired messages, permissions and responses. Informality may be useful without being uniquely Chinese or an authorized substitute for official negotiation.

baseline.claim: Humor, self-deprecation, and acknowledgment of minor errors can build rapport or preempt criticism, making later changes in tone more salient to foreign counterparts.
baseline.evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; Nixon and Kissinger memoir impressions; American interview recollections.
baseline.historical_anchor: Mao–Nixon, February 21, 1972; Deng's apology to George Bush in the Deng–Kissinger record, October 19, 1975; Kissinger–Qiao, November 13, 1972.
baseline.test: Trace changes in conversational tone, participant perceptions, and substantive bargaining in the same relationship. Compare first-time and experienced counterparts and different Chinese officials. Seek evidence connecting rapport to an identifiable concession rather than treating personal warmth as success.
baseline.caveat: Politeness, sincere error correction, personality, and shared humor are alternatives to calculated influence. The chapter's comparisons with Soviet humor are subjective and do not independently establish national cultural differences.

baseline_scope.author_period_and_domain: Principal empirical period 1967–1984, principally American–Chinese high political negotiation while Beijing sought a constructive relationship; application to future confrontation was explicitly left open. The claim-specific qualification below also applies.
baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: Politeness, sincere error correction, personality, and shared humor are alternatives to calculated influence. The chapter's comparisons with Soviet humor are subjective and do not independently establish national cultural differences.

assessments.tested_component: Humor or self-deprecation producing rapport that changes later expectations or concessions.

supporting_evidence.observation: Zhu’s public gift/campaign-contribution joke accompanied a substantive argument about Chinese reform interests.
supporting_evidence.limit: A public joke is the observed component, not a measured effect.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: No linked evidence shows humor altered a counterpart’s expectations or subsequent offer. There is no independent contrary test; absence of that link is not proof humor has no effect.

baseline.claim: PRC leaders use relations with third powers and rival foreign political figures to advertise alternatives, influence the counterpart's sense of dependence, and improve their bargaining position.
baseline.evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; contemporary event narratives; strategic interpretation, including explicitly conditional reasoning about 1969.
baseline.historical_anchor: Zhou–Kissinger, July 10–11, 1971; Deng–Kissinger, November 26, 1974; Mao–Kissinger, October 21, 1975; Kissinger–Huang Zhen, August 18, 1976; Reagan's meetings with PRC leaders, April 27, 1984.
baseline.test: Establish the alternative relationship's independent value, its timing relative to bargaining, explicit references to it, and counterpart responses. Compare genuine policy shifts with demonstrative gestures and distinguish domestic political rivals from international alternatives.
baseline.caveat: The proposed role of the March 1969 clashes in creating a wider coalition is conditional in Solomon's account. Domestic politics and genuine security interests also explain third-party actions. The Soviet helicopter-release footnote expressly leaves its internal dynamics unresolved.

baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: The proposed role of the March 1969 clashes in creating a wider coalition is conditional in Solomon's account. Domestic politics and genuine security interests also explain third-party actions. The Soviet helicopter-release footnote expressly leaves its internal dynamics unresolved.

assessments.tested_component: Advertising third-power alternatives to change the counterpart’s perceived dependence.

supporting_evidence.observation: Analyses identify alternative suppliers and Russia’s changing external outlets.
supporting_evidence.limit: Material alternatives do not prove a deliberate message or its reception.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: American diplomacy also introduced summit sequence and the Soviet relationship.
contrary_or_limiting_evidence.limit: A counterpart comparison, not a refutation of Chinese use.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: Need a dated Chinese invocation, recipient belief update and altered terms. The corpus does not isolate leverage from real security/economic interests or third-party agency.

baseline.claim: PRC officials may delay substantive movement until leadership conditions or the wider strategic context permit a more favorable agreement, preserving talks in the meantime.
baseline.evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; historical narrative; informal comments as reported by the author; retrospective causal interpretation.
baseline.historical_anchor: Vance's August 1977 Beijing visit; Huang Hua–Woodcock, November 14, 1977; Pu Shouchang–Hummel, March 18, 1982; Zhang Zai–Freeman, March 22, 1982; Pu Shouchang–Freeman, March 24, 1982.
baseline.test: Reconstruct periods of inactivity against changes in instructions, leadership authority, substantive positions, and external conditions. Identify evidence that an acceptable agreement existed but was deliberately deferred. Compare deliberate waiting with bureaucratic processing or irreconcilable interests.
baseline.caveat: Observed slowness does not identify its cause. The chapter relies partly on hindsight and foreign officials' interpretations of internal politics; apparent rigidity may reflect substantive preference rather than leadership conflict or a calculated delay.

baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: Observed slowness does not identify its cause. The chapter relies partly on hindsight and foreign officials' interpretations of internal politics; apparent rigidity may reflect substantive preference rather than leadership conflict or a calculated delay.

assessments.tested_component: Deliberate preservation of talks until leadership or strategic circumstances improve.

supporting_evidence.observation: Talks and political endorsement continued while commercial closure remained incomplete.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: Technical review and a similarly long EU process illustrate alternatives to strategic waiting.
A counterpart’s missing authorization also delayed settlement.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: Duration and eventual agreement cannot identify intentional delay. Need earlier acceptable offers, instructions to wait and the strategic or leadership change that released them.

baseline.claim: PRC negotiators can obtain partial agreements while explicitly reserving unresolved positions, and can preserve compromise options through wording that avoids a conspicuous reversal.
baseline.evidence_type: Agreement and memcon descriptions; interpretive discussion of credibility; strategic analogy without a standalone example.
baseline.historical_anchor: Unilateral paragraphs in the Shanghai Communiqué; Deng–Woodcock, December 15, 1978; Hua Guofeng's unilateral statement following normalization.
baseline.test: List issues settled, deferred, expressly reserved, or left ambiguous. Track whether later demands invoke those reservations and whether deferral stabilizes cooperation or increases leverage. Compare public rigidity with actual draft revisions and compromises.
baseline.caveat: An explicit reservation is not concealment and does not show agreement on the reserved issue. Solomon admits that normalization was not a fully specified plan and contrasts political credibility concerns with commercial retreats. The Sun-tzu explanation is an analogy, not demonstrated transmission of a military rule.

baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: An explicit reservation is not concealment and does not show agreement on the reserved issue. Solomon admits that normalization was not a fully specified plan and contrasts political credibility concerns with commercial retreats. The Sun-tzu explanation is an analogy, not demonstrated transmission of a military rule.

assessments.tested_component: Partial agreement with explicitly reserved issues; face-preserving wording treated as a separate unproved component.

supporting_evidence.observation: Normalization proceeded while U.S. arms sales remained expressly disputed.
Crew departure did not settle responsibility or all aircraft arrangements.
Reserved boundary areas were settled in a later instrument.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: Enforcement was still substantively incomplete after the partial package was announced.
contrary_or_limiting_evidence.limit: A partial announcement is not a completed agreement on its own reserved terms.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: Retain demonstrated partial settlement, not an inferred mechanism of saving face or concealed future concessions. Establish each reservation and its subsequent treatment separately.

baseline.claim: PRC negotiators can increase pressure through explicit threats, limited costly confrontations, or expanded demands, with the form and willingness to act changing as the relationship develops.
baseline.evidence_type: Narrative comparison across negotiation phases; American interview assessments; memcon-anchored cultural-exchange dispute.
baseline.historical_anchor: Relative absence of overt threats before 1979 versus their prominence in the 1981 arms-sales dispute; Habib–Han Xu exchanges, March 19, 20, 23, and 25, 1975, preceding cancellation of a performing-arts tour.
baseline.test: Record each threatened condition, consequence, material cost, implementation, retreat, and negotiated outcome. Test whether progressively disclosed requirements were new demands. Compare relationship stage, issue salience, domestic politics, and relative power as explanations for escalation.
baseline.caveat: Solomon states both that threats were sometimes abandoned and that some were carried out. The 1975 tour failed, and its factional purpose is disputed within the chapter. Neither threat issuance nor a canceled exchange proves bargaining success.

baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: Solomon states both that threats were sometimes abandoned and that some were carried out. The 1975 tour failed, and its factional purpose is disputed within the chapter. Neither threat issuance nor a canceled exchange proves bargaining success.

assessments.tested_component: Explicit pressure and conditional threats as conduct, not measured success or a national monopoly.

supporting_evidence.observation: China conditioned negotiated outcomes on the absence of additional U.S. sanctions/tariffs.
Defense contact was publicly withheld under political conditions.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: The United States also used and implemented tariff pressure; its deadlines and demands changed.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: Retain the repertoire. Specific Chinese concessions extracted through a threat, calibrated military coercion and relationship-driven changes in threat effectiveness require separate causal evidence.

baseline.claim: Foreign officials invested in a positive relationship with China may receive concentrated pressure because PRC leaders expect them to work hardest to preserve it.
baseline.evidence_type: Memcon and letter excerpts; narrative accounts of visits; author interpretation of reputational and relational incentives.
baseline.historical_anchor: Kissinger's treatment during the 1975 Ford-visit preparations; Bush's August 1980 visit; Deng–Bush, May 8, 1982; Zhao–Bush letter, January 20, 1981.
baseline.test: Compare pressure on established friends and skeptical officials facing the same issue, controlling for office, access, and negotiating authority. Measure whether friendly status brings greater access, harsher demands, more concessions, or improved ability to resist pressure.
baseline.caveat: Guanxi is Solomon's principal cultural explanation, but reputational investment and expected policy influence offer practical alternatives. The chapter also reports PRC weakness in reaching hostile Americans, so concentrated contact may reflect access limitations rather than superior manipulation.

baseline_scope.author_period_and_domain: Principal empirical period 1967–1984, principally American–Chinese high political negotiation while Beijing sought a constructive relationship; application to future confrontation was explicitly left open. The claim-specific qualification below also applies.
baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: Guanxi is Solomon's principal cultural explanation, but reputational investment and expected policy influence offer practical alternatives. The chapter also reports PRC weakness in reaching hostile Americans, so concentrated contact may reflect access limitations rather than superior manipulation.

assessments.tested_component: Concentrated pressure on friendly officials because of their investment in the relationship.

supporting_evidence.observation: A sympathetic old interlocutor was urged to contribute to better relations.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: Private status and acknowledged advice do not demonstrate pressured concession or fear of losing status.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: No recovered comparison of friendly and hostile counterparts identifies differential pressure or its effect. Availability and policy affinity remain sufficient alternatives.

baseline.claim: PRC leaders can invoke popular sentiment or the political vulnerability of accommodating officials as a limit on their flexibility and a reason for the counterpart to concede.
baseline.evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; author interpretation of domestic political constraints; competing explanations of the 1975 cultural dispute.
baseline.historical_anchor: Deng–Haig, June 16, 1981; Deng–Mondale, November 22, 1981; 1975 performing-arts dispute; post-Mao references to public feelings on Taiwan.
baseline.test: Compare claims of domestic constraint with available evidence of elite disagreement, institutional authorization, public mobilization, and later policy change. Distinguish a real constraint, selective presentation of one, and an unsupported bargaining assertion.
baseline.caveat: Solomon explicitly cannot determine whether some warnings are hollow and compares them with American invocation of Congress. The asserted change in popular influence under Deng is a period-specific interpretation, not a general model of how public opinion controls PRC policy.

baseline_scope.author_period_and_domain: Principal empirical period 1967–1984, principally American–Chinese high political negotiation while Beijing sought a constructive relationship; application to future confrontation was explicitly left open. The claim-specific qualification below also applies.
baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: Solomon explicitly cannot determine whether some warnings are hollow and compares them with American invocation of Congress. The asserted change in popular influence under Deng is a period-specific interpretation, not a general model of how public opinion controls PRC policy.

assessments.tested_component: Invoking public sentiment or an accommodating official’s vulnerability to induce concessions.

supporting_evidence.observation: The Chinese published accession narrative associates the post-bombing pause with dignity.
supporting_evidence.limit: Editorial interpretation, not an internal instruction or complete public-opinion record.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: American officials invoked independent congressional authority.
contrary_or_limiting_evidence.limit: Actual institutional constraint and tactical invocation can coexist on either side.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: Need the specific Chinese appeal, contemporaneous assessment of domestic constraint and foreign response. Neither later internet commentary nor a public dignity claim alone tests efficacy.

baseline.claim: Negotiating tone varies with individuals, assigned roles, senior instructions, and domestic circumstances; alternating harder and more accommodating presentations can affect expectations about compromise.
baseline.evidence_type: Memoir and interview impressions; memcon-based personality sketches; comparison of the same official across periods.
baseline.historical_anchor: Huang Hua's accommodating role in Kissinger's early exchanges versus his harder presentation in 1978–1982; Zhou's deference to Mao; Qiao's October 1975 and October 8, 1976, encounters with Kissinger.
baseline.test: Compare each individual's behavior across roles, issues, and leadership periods, and different negotiators operating under the same authority. Code tone separately from actual offer changes. Seek evidence of instructions before attributing a hard–soft pairing to orchestration.
baseline.caveat: The chapter calls the hard–soft tactic universal and notes that Deng could be abrasive while Huang could be conciliatory. The portraits are American-facing and partly impressionistic. Unresolved Mao–Zhou politics limit certainty about who directed every presentation.

baseline_scope.author_period_and_domain: Principal empirical period 1967–1984, principally American–Chinese high political negotiation while Beijing sought a constructive relationship; application to future confrontation was explicitly left open. The claim-specific qualification below also applies.
baseline_scope.claim_specific_qualification: The chapter calls the hard–soft tactic universal and notes that Deng could be abrasive while Huang could be conciliatory. The portraits are American-facing and partly impressionistic. Unresolved Mao–Zhou politics limit certainty about who directed every presentation.

assessments.tested_component: Variation in tone across individuals, instructions and roles, and its effect on expectations.

supporting_evidence.observation: Conrad’s interviews describe a shift from climate specialists to the premier’s foreign-policy team.
supporting_evidence.limit: Retrospective explanatory account without released mandates.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: Warm personal presentation coexisted with firm substantive demands.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: No sufficiently paired same-person or assigned-role comparison establishes orchestrated hard–soft tactics or a resulting concession. Tone and proposal changes must be coded separately.

baseline.claim: PRC officials use public communication around negotiations to establish agendas, raise or reduce expectations, advertise limits, and suggest openings, with different outlets offering different degrees of commitment.
baseline.evidence_type: Press interviews and statements; memcon excerpts; memoir descriptions of media arrangements; author inferences about audience effects.
baseline.historical_anchor: Carter–Deng, January 29, 1979; Deng–Kissinger, November 25, 1974; Deng–Ford, December 3, 1975; Haig–Huang Hua, October 30, 1981; Lin–Roy, July 25, 1978; Ji Chaozhu–U.S. Embassy Officer, March 2, 1982.
baseline.test: Connect public messages to private offers and identified audiences. Code outlet authority for the relevant period and distinguish agenda effects, domestic defense, expectation management, and actual concessions. Include instances of preserved confidentiality and publicity that releases pressure.
baseline.caveat: Solomon documents learning about television, failed expectation-raising, and respect for some confidentiality requests. The historical media hierarchy is not automatically valid later. His suggestion that a Chinese press criticism influenced the Mayaguez response is conjectural and needs independent causal evidence.

The historical media hierarchy is not automatically valid later. His suggestion that a Chinese press criticism influenced the Mayaguez response is conjectural and needs independent causal evidence.

assessments.tested_component: Public communication used to characterize the agenda, prior obligations and permissible movement.

supporting_evidence.observation: White papers and briefing defended different stages of the negotiation.
English and Chinese presentations supported immediate crew return while responsibility remained disputed.

contrary_or_limiting_evidence.observation: The U.S. publication dispute shows counterpart publicity and disputed effects too.

assessments.unresolved_remainder: Retain observable public positioning. A contemporary outlet hierarchy, internal dissemination and causal effects on public pressure need direct evidence rather than projection of Solomon’s older media categories.

baseline.claim: Rapid collection and internal circulation of foreign reporting can inform PRC bargaining while also generating domestic reactions that constrain negotiators or intensify later responses.
baseline.evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; personal communications; press-based reconstruction of feedback; admitted uncertainty about editorial selection.
baseline.historical_anchor: Zhang Wenjin–Holdridge, January 11, 1982; Zhang–Freeman, September 9, 1981; Deng–Haig, June 16, 1981; Deng–Mondale, November 22, 1981; June–July 1983 coverage of arms-sales protests.
baseline.test: Trace what reporting reached which institutions, when, and with what interpretation. Compare foreign publication, Chinese internal circulation, subsequent official discussion, and policy response. Distinguish exposure to information from accurate understanding and from actual political constraint.

baseline.claim: Openly specifying differences can coexist with limited cooperation, reassuring domestic and allied audiences while clarifying the common interests that sustain an agreement.

baseline.claim: Control over the schedule and apparent willingness to wait can help PRC negotiators exploit the counterpart's deadline, but Chinese negotiators are also susceptible to time pressure.
baseline.evidence_type: Memcon excerpts; memoir account of mutual deadline bargaining; comparison of Chinese, American, and British timing advantages.
baseline.historical_anchor: Huang Hua–Woodcock, July 5 and 14, 1978; Qiao–Kissinger, February 24–25, 1972; Carter–Chai Zemin, September 19, 1978; Vance–Huang Hua, October 3, 1978; abandoned February 28, 1982, target; PRC Hong Kong deadline announcement, November 9, 1983.
baseline.test: Identify who set each deadline, its credibility, who could walk away, timing of concessions, and consequences of expiry. Compare actual urgency with rhetoric of patience. Include deadlines ignored without agreement and cases in which Beijing faces greater time costs.
baseline.caveat: Kissinger described both sides using the 1972 deadline. The United States declined an unfavorable deal in February 1982, and Solomon recognizes initial British time leverage over Hong Kong. Cultural reserve does not establish an inherent Chinese advantage in patience.
